theme.text: The regulatory process surrounding glyphosate is heavily influenced by industry, leading to safety assessments that do not accurately reflect real-world exposure risks.

thesis.text: Regulators need to completely reassess their position on glyphosate safety due to the influence of industry data and the inadequacy of current safety limits.

pillars.label: Industry influence on regulation
pillars.text: Industry has shaped nearly every step of the regulatory process regarding glyphosate safety assessments.

pillars.label: Inadequate testing of formulations
pillars.text: Regulators largely assess glyphosate in isolation rather than testing the commercial products that people are actually exposed to.

pillars.label: Toxicity of co-formulants
pillars.text: Commercial formulations of glyphosate can be up to a thousand times more toxic than glyphosate alone due to additional ingredients.

pillars.label: Long-term effects of glyphosate
pillars.text: Even minuscule doses of glyphosate herbicides can result in serious disease over time, including cancer.

pillars.label: Regulatory reliance on industry data
pillars.text: Regulatory agencies rely heavily on industry-sponsored research when deciding whether glyphosate is safe, leading to similar conclusions across agencies.

pillars.label: Need for reassessment of safety limits
pillars.text: Current safety limits for glyphosate are not protective enough and need to be drastically reduced based on independent research findings.

mintedClaims.claimText: Glyphosate has remained one of the world’s most widely used herbicides due to industry influence on the regulatory process.
Industry’s influence extends from the studies regulators rely on and the products they test to the exposure limits they consider safe.
One of the biggest flaws in glyphosate regulation is that agencies largely assess glyphosate by itself, in isolation, instead of testing the commercial products people are actually exposed to.
Regulators do not require long-term toxicity testing of complete glyphosate formulations.
Even minuscule doses of glyphosate herbicides can result in serious disease over time, including cancer.
Independent studies often receive little or no attention compared to industry-sponsored research, which influences regulatory decisions.
Regulatory agencies do not take into account the cocktails of pesticides that people are exposed to daily.
The current acceptable daily intake of glyphosate is clearly inaccurate or wrong, according to Antoniou.
Antoniou's laboratory has reported DNA damage and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease in animals exposed to extremely low concentrations of commercial glyphosate formulations.
Regulators need to completely reassess their position on glyphosate safety due to the influence of industry data.
Antoniou criticized the growing use of glyphosate as a pre-harvest drying agent, which leads to glyphosate residues in the food supply.
The same biological pathway targeted by glyphosate exists in many bacteria and fungi, including those in the human gut microbiome.
The gut microbiome plays a vital role in digestion, immune function, cardiovascular health and nervous system signaling, Antoniou said.
Evidence from independent researchers also shows harmful effects can occur at doses regulators continue to describe as “absolutely safe,” Antoniou said.

If regulators evaluated the complete formulations instead of glyphosate alone, Antoniou said allowable exposure limits would have to be drastically reduced, and uses in homes, parks and other urban areas would likely be banned.

Regulatory agencies rely on laboratory animal toxicity studies to set their so-called safe exposure limits, but the criteria by which a given animal toxicity study is eligible to be considered were set by industry.
As a result, independent studies often receive little or no attention, even when they clearly have no conflicts of interest, Antoniou said.
That’s how influential industry has been, he said.
Even if regulators relied on stronger science, they would still be evaluating glyphosate under conditions that don’t match the real world, Antoniou said.
But you and I, we’re all exposed to cocktails of pesticides on a daily basis, he said.
This is another reason why our regulators are letting us down, Antoniou said. They’re not protecting us properly.
Manufacturers encourage farmers to spray wheat, barley, oats, rye and other crops just days before harvest so the grain dries more uniformly and can be harvested sooner.
The result is that glyphosate residues are going straight into the humans’ food supply, he said.
According to Antoniou, industry has long defended glyphosate by arguing that it targets a biological pathway found in plants but not in humans.
But that argument overlooks a critical piece of biology, he said.
Research from Antoniou’s laboratory and others shows glyphosate can disrupt those microbial communities, contributing to gut imbalance and the onset or the occurrence of leaky gut.
Monsanto clearly ignored this mechanism of toxicity, he said.
Evidence from independent researchers also shows harmful effects can occur at doses regulators continue to describe as absolutely safe, Antoniou said.
His laboratory has reported DNA damage and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease in animals exposed to extremely low concentrations of commercial glyphosate formulations.
In one study, animals developed liver disease after long-term exposure to glyphosate concentrations 125,000 times below the European Union safety limit and 250,000 times below the U.S. safety limit.

theme.text: The regulation of glyphosate is influenced by industry practices that compromise public health and safety.

thesis.text: Regulatory agencies need to reassess glyphosate safety due to significant flaws in current testing and evaluation methods.

pillars.label: Industry influence on regulation
pillars.text: Industry has shaped nearly every step of the regulatory process regarding glyphosate.

pillars.label: Flaws in glyphosate testing
pillars.text: Regulatory agencies largely assess glyphosate in isolation, ignoring the commercial products people are actually exposed to.

pillars.label: Toxicity of glyphosate formulations
pillars.text: Commercial formulations of glyphosate can be up to a thousand times more toxic than glyphosate alone.

pillars.label: Long-term effects of glyphosate
pillars.text: Even minuscule doses of glyphosate can result in serious diseases over time.

pillars.label: Need for reassessment of safety limits
pillars.text: Existing safety limits for glyphosate are not protective enough and need to be drastically reduced.

hostSignals.claimText: Glyphosate is one of the world’s most widely used herbicides due to industry influence on the regulatory process.
Regulatory agencies assess glyphosate primarily in isolation rather than in the context of commercial products.
Manufacturers add co-formulants to glyphosate that increase its toxicity.
Commercial formulations of glyphosate can be up to a thousand times more toxic than glyphosate alone.
Regulators do not require long-term toxicity testing of complete glyphosate formulations.
Even low concentrations of glyphosate can lead to serious health issues over time.
Regulatory agencies have relied on industry-sponsored research to assess glyphosate safety.
The current acceptable daily intake of glyphosate is likely inaccurate and should be much lower.
Glyphosate can disrupt gut microbiome, contributing to health issues.
Regulators do not take into account the combined exposure to multiple pesticides.
The effects of glyphosate exposure can take years to manifest, complicating the link to diseases.
Regulators need to completely reassess their position on glyphosate safety due to reliance on questionable data.

packets.claimUnits: Glyphosate has remained one of the world’s most widely used herbicides not because the science supports its safety, but because industry has shaped nearly every step of the regulatory process, molecular geneticist and toxicologist Michael Antoniou, Ph.D. , said this week.
packets.localResponseWindow: In an interview on “ The Corbett Report ,” Antoniou outlined what he sees as the biggest failures that have kept the “deceptively toxic” herbicide on the market despite a growing body of independent research linking it to serious health risks. packets.claimUnits: One of the biggest flaws in glyphosate regulation is that agencies largely assess glyphosate by itself, in isolation — instead of testing the commercial products people are actually exposed to, Antoniou said.
packets.attributionLeadIn: “That is not science,” he said. “That is really an act of deception.”
packets.quoteOrSpeakerBlock: ‘Massive act of negligence’ is ‘putting public health at risk’ One of the biggest flaws in glyphosate regulation is that agencies largely assess glyphosate by itself, in isolation — instead of testing the commercial products people are actually exposed to, Antoniou said. Manufacturers add chemicals known as co-formulants that “basically punch holes in the plant cell walls,” so glyphosate can enter and destroy the plant.

packets.claimText: Even low concentrations of glyphosate can lead to serious health issues over time.
packets.claimUnits: His laboratory has reported DNA damage and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease in animals exposed to extremely low concentrations of commercial glyphosate formulations.
packets.attributionLeadIn: Evidence from independent researchers also shows harmful effects can occur at doses regulators continue to describe as “absolutely safe,” Antoniou said.
packets.localResponseWindow: In one study, animals developed liver disease after long-term exposure to glyphosate concentrations “125,000 times below the European Union safety limit and 250,000 times below the U.S. safety limit.” “Even minuscule doses of glyphosate herbicides, given enough time, can result in serious disease,” Antoniou said. packets.claimText: Regulatory agencies have relied on industry-sponsored research to assess glyphosate safety.
packets.claimUnits: He said regulatory agencies around the world rely heavily on industry-sponsored research when deciding whether glyphosate is safe.
packets.attributionLeadIn: Testing only glyphosate is just one example of how industry has shaped regulation, according to Antoniou.
packets.quoteOrSpeakerBlock: Testing only glyphosate is just one example of how industry has shaped regulation, according to Antoniou. He said regulatory agencies around the world rely heavily on industry-sponsored research when deciding whether glyphosate is safe. Because regulators often use the same industry data, they reach similar conclusions and cite one another as supporting evidence. Antoniou pointed to a widely cited 2000 study in Regulatory Toxicology and Pharmacology that concluded glyphosate posed no significant safety concerns.
packets.localResponseWindow: Because regulators often use the same industry data, they reach similar conclusions and cite one another as supporting evidence. Antoniou pointed to a widely cited 2000 study in Regulatory Toxicology and Pharmacology that concluded glyphosate posed no significant safety concerns. Regulatory agencies relied on that paper for years. Earlier this year, however, the paper was retracted after evidence showed its authors had undisclosed conflicts of interest. Even more troubling, Antoniou said, “they had solid evidence that actually this paper wasn’t even written by the authors. It was ghostwritten…

packets.claimText: The current acceptable daily intake of glyphosate is likely inaccurate and should be much lower.
packets.claimUnits: “We cannot set an acceptable daily safe intake limit,” he said. “If I was to make an educated guess right now, I would say it would probably be in the order of about a thousand times lower than where we are at the moment.”
packets.attributionLeadIn: Existing safety limits are nowhere near protective enough, he said.
packets.localResponseWindow: Antoniou also rejected the idea that farmers cannot transition off of glyphosate . “There are alternatives,” he said. “All it takes is the political will to support these initiatives, to really move towards a sustainable, robust and safe agricultural system.” Looking back at glyphosate’s history, Antoniou said the herbicide “was always touted by industry as the safest-ever pesticide of any sort ever invented. … If the … so-called safest pesticide … is this bad, deceptively toxic, what about all the rest?” he asked. “It really paints a very dark picture for pesticides in general.”

packets.claimText: Glyphosate can disrupt gut microbiome, contributing to health issues.
packets.claimUnits: The same pathway exists in many bacteria and fungi, including microorganisms that make up the human gut microbiome .

Evidence from independent researchers also shows harmful effects can occur at doses regulators continue to describe as “absolutely safe,” Antoniou said. packets.claimText: Regulators do not take into account the combined exposure to multiple pesticides.
packets.claimUnits: “But you and I, we’re all exposed to cocktails of pesticides on a daily basis,” he said. “Tens of different pesticides we can be exposed to on a daily basis through our food supply. Does the regulator take that into account? Not at all.”
packets.attributionLeadIn: Even if regulators relied on stronger science, they would still be evaluating glyphosate under conditions that don’t match the real world, Antoniou said.
packets.localResponseWindow: That gap has become even more important as weeds have become resistant to glyphosate, and farmers increasingly spray chemical cocktails , including glyphosate, 2,4-D and dicamba , he said. packets.attributionLeadIn: “What this study tells us is clearly … first of all, glyphosate and glyphosate herbicides are definitely carcinogenic,” Antoniou said. “And also, clearly, the current acceptable daily intake … is clearly inaccurate or wrong.”
packets.localResponseWindow: “The effects can take time to manifest,” he said. theme.text: Public health narratives about vaccines are often challenged by claims of misinformation and censorship.

thesis.text: The claims made by public health authorities regarding vaccines lack credible scientific support and are often based on misinformation.

pillars.label: Vaccination Rates and Exemptions
pillars.text: Half of American school children are not fully vaccinated, and at least 1 in 88 toddlers are completely unvaccinated.

pillars.label: Public Health Messaging
pillars.text: The Jefferson County Public Health ad attempted to reassure parents about vaccines through light-hearted content.

pillars.label: Claims About Vaccine Safety
pillars.text: The ad claims that vaccines are tested more than any other medicine.

pillars.label: Vaccine Exemptions
pillars.text: There is a rise in the rate of parents seeking vaccine exemptions for their children.

pillars.label: Thimerosal and Vaccine Safety
pillars.text: Thimerosal, a mercury-based preservative used in vaccines, is toxic and has been linked to neurological damage.

pillars.label: Aluminum in Vaccines
pillars.text: Aluminum in vaccines is toxic and can cause neurological damage.

pillars.label: SIDS and Vaccination
pillars.text: SIDS became the leading cause of post-neonatal mortality in the U.S. following the introduction of mass vaccination programs.

pillars.label: Censorship and Vaccine Debate
pillars.text: There is a pattern of censorship regarding discussions about vaccine safety and efficacy.

theme.text: Public health narratives about vaccines are often challenged by alternative perspectives and claims regarding vaccine safety and efficacy.

thesis.text: The claims made by public health authorities regarding vaccines lack credible scientific support and are often based on misinformation.

pillars.label: Vaccination Rates and Parental Education
pillars.text: Half of American school children are not fully vaccinated, and at least 1 in 88 toddlers are completely unvaccinated, with parents who choose not to vaccinate typically being highly educated.

pillars.label: Claims in Public Health Ads
pillars.text: The Jefferson County Public Health ad claims that children face more challenges to their immune system while playing outside than from vaccines, and that vaccines are tested more than any other medicine.

pillars.label: Vaccine Exemptions
pillars.text: There is a rise in the rate of parents seeking vaccine exemptions for their children as childhood vaccination rates drop steadily across the country.

pillars.label: Thimerosal and Vaccine Safety
pillars.text: Thimerosal, a mercury-based preservative used in vaccines, is toxic and has been linked to neurological damage and autism.

pillars.label: Aluminum in Vaccines
pillars.text: Aluminum, used as an adjuvant in vaccines, is toxic and can cause neurological damage, and the levels in vaccines exceed safety limits established for other injectables.

pillars.label: SIDS and Vaccination
pillars.text: The introduction of mass vaccination programs in the U.S. coincided with a rise in Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS), which became the leading cause of post-neonatal mortality.

pillars.label: Censorship and Vaccine Discourse
pillars.text: Efforts to discuss vaccine safety and efficacy are often met with censorship and resistance from public health authorities and media outlets.

pillars.label: Chronic Illness Rates
pillars.text: The chronic illness rate in U.S. children has increased significantly since the 1986 National Childhood Vaccine Injury Act, with 54% of children diagnosed with a chronic health condition by 2011.
